author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: va
fields.label: UPS rating
fields.hint: From the UPS label or box, for example the VA or kVA figure. One kVA is a thousand VA.

fields.name: ah
fields.label: Battery capacity
fields.hint: From the battery label. Small computer UPS units have a built-in battery of a few Ah; home UPS units use an external tubular battery.

fields.name: load_w
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Total watts on the UPS. A desktop PC with a monitor is a few hundred watts, a router or fibre modem about ten, a small CCTV setup a few tens.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: UPS power factor
fields.hint: Line-interactive home UPS units are about 0.6; online UPS units about 0.8 to 1. Max watts = VA × power factor.

fields.name: inverter_eff
fields.label: Inverter efficiency
fields.hint: As a decimal. A typical home UPS is about 0.85.

fields.name: idle_w
fields.label: Inverter idle draw
fields.hint: What the UPS or inverter uses itself, even with nothing plugged in (no-load current × battery volts on its label). Not counted when inverter efficiency is one (a DC load).

fields.name: dod
fields.label: Usable depth of discharge
fields.hint: As a decimal: 0.5 means half the battery. Leave blank to use the value for your battery type.

answer: A {{in.va|int}} VA UPS with a {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery runs a {{in.load_w|int}} W desktop PC for about {{out.hours|hm}}. The UPS can deliver at most {{out.max_w|int}} W ({{in.va|int}} VA × {{out.pf|2}} power factor), so this load uses {{out.load_pct|int}}% of it. Backup hours = Ah × volts × usable depth ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw).
how: Capacity check: {{in.va}} VA × {{out.pf|2}} power factor = {{out.max_w|int}} W, and {{in.load_w}} W is {{out.load_pct|int}}% of that, so the UPS can run it. Backup: {{in.ah}} Ah × {{in.volts|1}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} usable = {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh in the battery. The battery gives {{in.load_w}} W ÷ {{out.inverter_eff|pct}} inverter efficiency + {{out.idle_w}} W the inverter draws itself = {{out.battery_w|1}} W. {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh ÷ {{out.battery_w|1}} W = {{out.hours|2}} hours, about {{out.hours|hm}}.
key_facts: UPS backup time in hours = battery Ah × battery volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw); the VA rating sets how big a load the UPS can carry, not how long it runs.

A line-interactive home UPS delivers about {{d.pf_ups_line_interactive|2}} W per VA, so a {{in.va|int}} VA (one kVA) UPS can run loads up to about {{out.max_w|int}} W; an online UPS delivers more watts per VA, so read the power factor on its label.

A {{in.va|int}} VA UPS on a {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery gives about {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W (a desktop PC), about {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W, and about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} for a {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W router and CCTV load on a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery.
The calculator refuses a load above VA × power factor instead of showing a shorter backup, because a real UPS trips on overload rather than running the load for less time.

formula.text: P_max = VA × PF (load must be ≤ P_max); t = (Ah × V × DoD) ÷ (P ÷ η + P_idle)
lines: P_max = the most watts the UPS can deliver
VA = UPS rating in volt-amperes, PF = UPS power factor
Ah = battery capacity, V = battery bank voltage
DoD = usable depth of discharge, η = inverter efficiency
P_idle = the inverter's own draw with no load (from its label; none for a DC load)

sections.h2: UPS backup time for a PC
p: A desktop PC with a monitor is about {{in.load_w|int}} W when working and more when gaming, so on a {{in.va|int}} VA UPS with a {{in.ah|int}} Ah tubular battery you get about {{out.hours|hm}}, enough to ride through a normal loadshedding slot or to save and shut down. A small office UPS with its built-in sealed battery of a few Ah gives only minutes; enter its Ah to see how few.

A gaming PC at {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W needs a bigger UPS, not just a bigger battery: a {{in.va|int}} VA line-interactive unit can only deliver about {{out.max_w|int}} W. A {{ex.2.in.va|int}} VA UPS delivers about {{ex.2.out.max_w|int}} W, and on two {{ex.2.in.ah|int}} Ah batteries at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V it runs the gaming PC for about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}}.

sections.h2: Why the load must fit the UPS rating first
p: A UPS has two limits. The VA rating with its power factor sets the largest load it can carry at any moment; the battery sets how long it can carry it. This tool checks the first limit before the second: if the load is more than VA × power factor, it shows an error instead of a backup time, because the UPS would trip on overload and run the load for no time at all.

Line-interactive home UPS units (the usual square-wave or modified sine wave units in Pakistan) are built for a power factor of about {{d.pf_ups_line_interactive|2}}, so a {{in.va|int}} VA unit delivers about {{out.max_w|int}} W. Online and better pure sine wave units deliver more watts per VA. Change the power factor under Advanced to match the label on your UPS.

mistakes: Reading VA as watts. A {{in.va|int}} VA line-interactive UPS delivers only about {{out.max_w|int}} W; a load above VA × power factor trips the UPS, and this tool rejects it for that reason.
Expecting hours from a small office UPS. Its built-in sealed battery holds a few Ah, so backup is minutes; long backup needs an external tubular or lithium battery.
Entering the PC's power supply rating as the load. A PC with a supply rated for several hundred watts usually draws far less; use a plug-in meter or the appliance load calculator.
Draining the battery fully. Tubular batteries should be used to about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}}; many UPS units cut off later than that, which gives longer backup but a shorter battery life.
Adding the Ah of batteries in series. Two batteries in series on a {{d.battery_v_default|int}} V UPS double the volts, not the Ah.
safety: Fit the battery with a fuse and correctly sized cable, keep lead-acid batteries ventilated, and have a licensed electrician connect a UPS to the house wiring.

faq.q: Which UPS do I need for a desktop computer?
faq.a: A desktop PC with a monitor is about {{in.load_w|int}} W, so a {{in.va|int}} VA line-interactive UPS ({{out.max_w|int}} W) runs it at {{out.load_pct|int}}% load. For long loadshedding backup pair it with an external tubular battery; a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery gives about {{out.hours|hm}}.

faq.q: How long will a UPS last for a PC?
faq.a: About {{out.hours|hm}} for a {{in.load_w|int}} W PC on a {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery, and about {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W with a fan added. A small office UPS with its own sealed battery lasts only minutes at this load.

faq.q: What is the UPS backup time for a Wi-Fi router during loadshedding?
faq.a: A router or fibre modem is about ten watts, so almost any UPS carries it; the battery decides the hours. A router with a small CCTV recorder, about {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W, runs about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} on a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery, and a router alone runs longer, though not in proportion: the UPS itself keeps drawing about {{data.appliances.ups-idle.running_w|int}} W.

faq.q: How much backup does a UPS give for CCTV?
faq.a: A DVR with a few cameras is a few tens of watts. On the {{ex.1.in.va|int}} VA UPS with a {{ex.1.in.ah|int}} Ah battery in the example, {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W of router and CCTV gives about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}}; enter your own camera count and watts for an exact figure.

faq.q: What is the backup time of a {{in.va|int}} VA (one kVA) UPS?
faq.a: It depends on the battery and the load, not the VA. With a {{in.ah|int}} Ah tubular battery a one kVA UPS gives about {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W and about {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W. The {{in.va|int}} VA rating only limits the load to about {{out.max_w|int}} W.

faq.q: What is the UPS battery backup calculation formula?
faq.a: Backup hours = battery Ah × battery volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw), after checking that the load is no more than VA × power factor. For a tubular battery use about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} usable and about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} efficiency; for lithium about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} usable.

faq.q: Which UPS is right for a gaming PC?
faq.a: A gaming PC can draw {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W or more, which is beyond a {{in.va|int}} VA line-interactive UPS. A {{ex.2.in.va|int}} VA unit delivers about {{ex.2.out.max_w|int}} W, and with two {{ex.2.in.ah|int}} Ah batteries at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V it gives about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}}. Choose a pure sine wave model for a PC power supply.
